s.d: to leap or spring up, presumably from a seated position
s.g: to leap up; to jump up

s.d: to cause someone to stand up
s.g: to cause to stand; to raise up

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: to cause someone to live again after having once died
s.g: to raise to life; to make live again

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Birth, Procreation
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to raise up seed) the male role in begetting children
s.g: to beget; to procreate; to become the father of
s.c: In contexts such as ⟦Matthew 22:24|Matthew 22:24⟧, ⟦Mark 12:19|Mark 12:19⟧, and ⟦Luke 20:28|Luke 20:28⟧ it may be important to add a note concerning levirate responsibilities, that is to say, the requirement for a younger brother to beget children by a deceased older brother’s wife and the reckoning of such an offspring as being the descendant of the older deceased brother.

s.dp: Stances and Events Related to Stances › Stand
s.d: to assume a standing position

s.dp: Linear Movement › Leave, Depart, Flee, Escape, Send
s.d: to move away from a reference point, with the possible implication of ‘getting up and leaving’
s.g: to depart; to go away from; to leave

s.d: to come into existence, with the implication of assuming a place or position
s.g: to come into existence; to appear; to arise

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: to come back to life after having once died
s.g: to come back to life; to live again; to be resurrected; resurrection
s.c: In a number of languages there is a difficulty involved in formulating some expression for ‘resurrection’ or ‘living again,’ since such a phrase may refer to what is technically known as metempsychosis, that is to say, the rebirth of the soul in another existence, a belief which is widely held in a number of areas of south Asia. This problem may be avoided in some languages by speaking of ‘his body will live again’ or ‘his body will come back to life’ or ‘he will be the same person when he lives again.’

s.d: to rise up in open defiance of authority, with the presumed intention to overthrow it or to act in complete opposition to its demands{N:001}
s.g: to rebel against; to revolt; to engage in insurrection; rebellion

s.d: to speak with considerable volume or loudness{N:001}
s.g: to cry out; to shout; to call out; to speak loudly

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἀνάχυσις ‘flood,’ not occurring in the NT) an extremely high point on a scale of extent and implying an excess of something with negative value
s.c: In some languages the equivalent of this phrase in ⟦1 Peter 4:4|1 Peter 4:4⟧ is ‘they lived very bad lives’ or ‘there was nothing bad that they didn’t do.’

s.dp: Linear Movement › Leave, Depart, Flee, Escape, Send
s.d: to move away from a location, implying a considerable distance
s.g: to withdraw; to retire; to go off; to go away

s.d: to move back to a point or area from which one has previously departed, but with more explicit emphasis upon the return (compare {L:ὑποστρέφω<SDBG:ὑποστρέφω:000000>}[a], {D:15.88})

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Relief from Trouble
s.d: relief from distressful, burdensome circumstances
s.c: In ⟦Acts 3:20|Acts 3:20⟧ the phrase καιροὶ ἀναψύξεως is generally regarded as a reference to the Messianic age.|In a number of languages it may be extremely difficult to speak of ‘relief coming from the Lord.’ It is easy enough to speak of animate beings ‘coming,’ but to have a state of relief ‘coming’ may be semantically impossible. However, the entire expression in ⟦Acts 3:20|Acts 3:20⟧ may be restructured as ‘so that the Lord may cause you to have relief from trouble’ or ‘… cause you to no longer be troubled.’ For another interpretation of ἀνάψυξις in ⟦Acts 3:20|Acts 3:20⟧, see LN 25.148.

s.d: a state of cheer and encouragement after a period of having been troubled or upset
s.c: For another interpretation of ἀνάψυξις in ⟦Acts 3:20|Acts 3:20⟧, see LN 22.35.

s.d: to cause someone to recover a state of cheer or encouragement after a time of anxiety and trouble
s.c: ἀναψύχω may be rendered idiomatically in a number of instances, for example, ‘to give one’s heart back to a person’ or ‘to make one’s heart feel strong again.’

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Sell, Buy, Price
s.d: one who sells persons as slaves, including one who kidnaps persons and sells them

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the brother of Simon Peter and one of the twelve apostles
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἀνδρίζομαι ‘to be manly’ or ‘to become a man,’ not occurring in the NT) to exhibit courage in the face of danger
s.g: to be brave; to be courageous

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person greeted in the Epistle to the Romans
a person who murders another person
pertaining to one who cannot be accused of anything wrong
s.c: In a number of languages the phrase ‘without accusations’ must be rendered by a clause, for example, ‘in such a way that no one can accuse you of doing wrong’ or ‘without the possibility of anyone accusing you.’

s.d: pertaining to that which cannot be fully related or communicated
pertaining to what cannot be uttered or expressed{N:001}
s.g: what cannot be expressed in words

s.d: pertaining to what will not go out of existence

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Patience, Endurance, Perseverance
s.d: pertaining to what can be borne or endured
s.c: In some languages ‘it will be more tolerable’ in ⟦Matthew 11:22|Matthew 11:22⟧ may be satisfactorily expressed as ‘it will be easier to bear’ or ‘the suffering will be less.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Mercy, Merciless
s.d: pertaining to the lack of mercy or the refusal to be merciful
s.c: The meaning of ἀνέλεος and ἀνελεήμων is often expressed in highly idiomatic ways, for example, ‘to refuse to look at,’ ‘to turn one’s back on,’ or ‘to refuse to hear a person’s cries for help.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Mercy, Merciless
s.d: pertaining to the lack of mercy or the refusal to be merciful
s.c: The meaning of ἀνέλεος and ἀνελεήμων is often expressed in highly idiomatic ways, for example, ‘to refuse to look at,’ ‘to turn one’s back on,’ or ‘to refuse to hear a person’s cries for help.’

s.dp: Linear Movement › Drive Along, Carry Along
s.d: to be caused to move by the wind
s.g: to be driven or carried about by the wind

s.d: air in relatively rapid movement, but without specification as to the force of the movement
s.c: As in the case of English (which has, for example, such terms as breeze, zephyr, gust, storm, whirlwind, cyclone, tornado, etc.), other languages likewise normally have a number of different terms depending upon the strength of the wind and whether the wind may be carrying substances such as sand or dust. In some languages there may also be a problem involved in the use of terms for ‘wind,’ since some of these may have meanings of malicious or malevolent spirits, or they may imply a disease-bringing event.

s.d: pertaining to not being possible, in the sense of not being in accord with human experience
s.c: In view of the double negation in ⟦Luke 17:1|Luke 17:1⟧, it may be better to translate ‘things that make people fall into sin are bound to happen.’ The derivative meaning of ἀνένδεκτος in the context of ⟦Luke 17:1|Luke 17:1⟧ is thus a matter of inevitability as based upon human experience (see LN 71.38).

s.dp: Understand › Ease or Difficulty in Understanding
s.d: pertaining to being impossible to understand on the basis of careful examination or investigation
s.g: impossible to understand; unfathomable; impossible to comprehend

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Patience, Endurance, Perseverance
s.d: pertaining to enduring difficulties without becoming angry or upset

s.dp: Understand › Ease or Difficulty in Understanding
s.d: pertaining to being impossible to understand on the basis of careful examination or investigation
s.g: impossible to understand; unfathomable; impossible to comprehend

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Shame, Disgrace, Humiliation
s.d: pertaining to having no reason or need for being ashamed or feeling disgrace
pertaining to what cannot be criticized
s.c: It may be necessary in some languages to restructure ἀκατάγνωστος and ἀνεπίλημπτος as complete clauses, so that instead of ‘sound words which are above criticism’ in ⟦Titus 2:8|Titus 2:8⟧, one may translate ‘sound words which no one can criticize’ or ‘… against which no one can say anything.’ ‘Above reproach’ in ⟦1 Timothy 6:14|1 Timothy 6:14⟧ may be rendered as ‘in such a way that no one can criticize it.’

s.d: to move up
s.g: to come up; to go up; to ascend
s.c: The upward movement may be of almost any gradient, for example, in going up a road to Jerusalem (⟦Galatians 1:17|Galatians 1:17⟧) or in going up into a tree (⟦Luke 19:4|Luke 19:4⟧) or in ascending into heaven (⟦Acts 2:34|Acts 2:34⟧).

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Relief from Trouble
s.d: relief as a cessation or suspension of trouble and difficulty
s.c: In rendering ‘relief to you who suffer,’ it may be necessary to restructure the semantic relations, for example, ‘to cause you who suffer not to have to suffer longer’ or ‘to cause you to no longer have to suffer.’

s.d: a partial degree of liberty or freedom{N:001}

s.dp: Courts and Legal Procedures › Judicial Hearing, Inquiry
s.d: to interrogate a defendant during a judicial hearing, often by means of torture or lashing
s.c: In the Roman legal system it was customary to use various forms of physical torture in order to extract confessions from persons who were not Romans and who had been charged with serious crimes, particularly crimes against the state.

s.d: a marker of negatively linked elements{N:001}
s.g: without; not with; no relationship to; apart from; independent of
s.c: The phrase ἄνευ τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν in ⟦Matthew 10:29|Matthew 10:29⟧ is elliptical, for it presumes some type of involvement by God in such an event. Some have interpreted the phrase ἄνευ τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν as meaning ‘without your Father’s consent,’ while others interpret it as meaning ‘without your Father’s knowledge.’ The particular manner or mode of involvement by God must depend upon the broader context and not upon the meaning of ἄνευ.|The phrase ἄνευ λόγου in ⟦1 Peter 3:1|1 Peter 3:1⟧ is semantically equivalent to an event, for it means essentially ‘without their saying a word’ or ‘without them saying anything.’

s.d: pertaining to something which should not or cannot be used

s.dp: Learn › Learn the Location of Something
s.d: to learn the location of something by intentional searching
s.g: to find by searching; to look for and find

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Patience, Endurance, Perseverance
s.d: to be patient with, in the sense of enduring possible difficulty
s.g: to be patient with; to have patience; patience

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Accept As True
s.d: to continue to accept as valid or true

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations of the Same Generation
s.d: the child of one’s uncle and aunt, either on the fathers side or the mothers side
s.c: Some languages make a clear distinction between so-called ‘parallel cousins’ and ‘cross cousins.’ Parallel cousins would be the offspring of one’s father’s brother or of one’s mother’s sister, while cross cousins would be the offspring of one’s father’s sister or of one’s mother’s brother. There is no way of knowing from the context of ⟦Colossians 4:10|Colossians 4:10⟧ what the specific relationship is between Mark and Barnabas, but for languages which have no general term for cousins, but only specific terms for parallel cousins or cross cousins, it is necessary to select one or another of these specific terms in speaking of Mark. By means of a footnote one can indicate that the Greek text does not specify which type of cousin is involved.

s.dp: Plants › Plants That Are Not Trees
s.d: annual plant that can reach 50 cm in height; has fine leaves; yellow flowers form a shape like a covered cup; leaves and seeds have a pleasant, spicy smell; Anethum graveolens; garden herb, used in cooking
s.c: In designating ‘dill’ as well as ἡδύοσμον ‘mint,’ πήγανον ‘rue,’ and κύμινον ‘cumin,’ it is probably wise to borrow a term and use a classifier, for example, ‘a seasoning herb called dill.’

s.d: to be fitting or right, with the implication of possible moral judgment involved
s.g: to be fitting; to be right

s.d: pertaining to fierceness, in the sense of being wild and untamed
an adult male person of marriageable age{N:001}
s.c: In some languages the equivalent of ‘now that I am a man’ is ‘now that I am grown’ or ‘now that I have become strong.’

s.d: a human being (normally an adult)
s.g: (in the singular) person; human being; individual; (in the plural) people; persons; mankind
s.c: In ⟦Matthew 14:35|Matthew 14:35⟧ (ἐπιγνόντες αὐτὸν οἱ ἄνδρες τοῦ τόπου ἐκείνου ‘when the people of that place recognized him’) one may argue that οἱ ἄνδρες refers specifically to males, but the context would seem to indicate that the reference is to people in general. In translation a pronominal expression may frequently be employed when ἀνήρ occurs in the text, for example, ‘when those who lived in that place recognized him.’|It is not uncommon in languages for a term which is often used to refer to an adult male to be employed also in a generic sense of ‘person.’ This is especially true when such terms are used in the plural form.|In a number of instances, generic meanings of receptor languages have not been recognized as such, since translators have assumed that such receptor-language terms refer only to members of a particular tribe or group (because they have been found only in specific contexts), while in reality such terms often designate people in general. One must, however, be on the alert for seemingly generic terms which refer only to the so-called ‘in-group,’ that is to say, members of a particular tribe, society, or community.|The parallelism in the ⟦Romans 4:8|Romans 4:8⟧ quotation from ⟦Psalms 32:1|Psalms 32:1⟧ indicates clearly that the reference of ἀνήρ is not a particular male but any person.

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Based upon Marriage
s.d: a man who is married to a woman
s.c: ἀνήρ in the meaning of ‘husband’ is normally clearly marked by context, usually involving a so- called ‘possessive marker,’ though in some contexts such as ⟦John 4:17|John 4:17⟧ and ⟦Matthew 19:10|Matthew 19:10⟧, the distinctions in meaning are quite clear, but it is only from each individual context that one can determine whether ἀνήρ means simply ‘man’ (see LN 9.24) or ‘husband.’ See also discussion at LN 10.54.

s.d: to oppose someone, involving not only a psychological attitude but also a corresponding behavior{N:001}
s.g: to oppose; to be hostile toward; to show hostility
s.c: In translating this phrase in ⟦Galatians 2:11|Galatians 2:11⟧ it may be appropriate in some languages to say ‘I spoke against him with other people present.’

s.d: to resist by actively opposing pressure or power
s.c: In a number of languages one may appropriately translate ‘to resist’ in a number of contexts as ‘to fight back against’ or ‘to oppose in return.’ In some contexts, however, such as ⟦Acts 7:51|Acts 7:51⟧, the meaning may perhaps be best expressed by a negation, for example, ‘you have never been willing to yield to the Holy Spirit.’

s.d: to acknowledge one’s thankfulness, restricted in NT usage to contexts in which God is the one being thanked
s.g: to thank; to give thanks to

s.d: the blossom of a plant
s.c: In some languages it may be difficult to use generic expressions such as ‘flower’ or ‘plant.’ One may therefore be obliged to use a more specific designation of a type of flower which lasts for only a day or so. In ⟦James 1:10|James 1:10⟧ it is the fragile and temporary nature of the blossom which is important in this figurative context.

The occurrence of ἀνθρακιά ‘charcoal fire’ in ⟦John 18:18|John 18:18⟧ fits the context well, since a charcoal fire provides a maximum of heat with a minimum of smoke. The making and use of charcoal is widespread throughout the world, and there is generally no difficulty in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘charcoal.’ However, where such a term does not exist, it is possible to speak of ‘a wood fire’ or simply ‘a fire.’

ἄνθραξ occurs in the NT only in ⟦Romans 12:20|Romans 12:20⟧ in the adage ἄνθρακας πυρὸς σωρεύσεις ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ ‘heap coals of fire on his head.’ This idiomatic expression probably refers to making someone blush with shame and remorse (see LN 25.199).|In rendering ἄνθρακας πυρός it is not necessary to use a word which specifically refers to ‘flaming charcoal.’ What is important is that the embers be understood as ‘fiery embers’ or ‘hot ashes’ or ‘burning ashes.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Acceptable To, To Be Pleased With
s.d: pertaining to causing people to be pleased, with the implication of being in contrast to God or at the sacrifice of some principle
s.c: The expression ‘men-pleasers’ may often be rendered as ‘those who are just trying to make people like them.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:ἄνθρωπος<SDBG:ἄνθρωπος:000000>}[a] ‘people,’ {D:9.1}) pertaining to being a person
s.c: Many languages, however, lack an adjectival form equivalent to ‘human,’ and therefore one may speak of ‘human wisdom’ as being ‘wisdom that people have.’ At the same time, languages may actually lack an abstract term such as ‘wisdom,’ and therefore it may be necessary to translate ‘taught by human wisdom’ as ‘taught by those people who are wise.’

s.d: (an idiom, literally: human hand) a human being as a means of accomplishing something
a person who murders another person
a human being (normally an adult)
s.g:
(in the singular) person, human being, individual; (in the plural) people, persons,
 mankind
s.c: In ⟦Matthew 14:35|Matthew 14:35⟧ (ἐπιγνόντες αὐτὸν οἱ ἄνδρες τοῦ τόπου ἐκείνου ‘when the people of that place recognized him’) one may argue that οἱ ἄνδρες refers specifically to males, but the context would seem to indicate that the reference is to people in general. In translation a pronominal expression may frequently be employed when ἀνήρ occurs in the text, for example, ‘when those who lived in that place recognized him’.|It is not uncommon in languages for a term which is often used to refer to an adult male to be employed also in a generic sense of ‘person.’ This is especially true when such terms are used in the plural form.|In a number of instances, generic meanings of receptor languages have not been recognized as such, since translators have assumed that such receptor-language terms refer only to members of a particular tribe or group (because they have been found only in specific contexts), while in reality such terms often designate people in general. One must, however, be on the alert for seemingly generic terms which refer only to the so-called ‘in-group,’ that is to say, members of a particular tribe, society, or community.

s.d: an adult male person of marriageable age{N:001}

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Based upon Marriage
s.d: a man who is married to a woman
s.c: ἀνήρ in the meaning of ‘husband’ is normally clearly marked by context, usually involving a so- called ‘possessive marker,’ though in some contexts such as ⟦John 4:17|John 4:17⟧ and ⟦Matthew 19:10|Matthew 19:10⟧, the distinctions in meaning are quite clear, but it is only from each individual context that one can determine whether ἀνήρ means simply ‘man’ (see LN 9.24) or ‘husband.’ See also discussion at LN 10.54.

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Body
s.d: (an idiom, literally: the outside person) the physical nature or aspect of a person
s.c: The phrase ὁ ἔξω ἄνθρωπος is to be understood in direct contrast with ὁ ἔσω (ἄνθρωπος) in the same verse, which refers to the psychological or spiritual nature of human personality (see LN 26.1).

s.d: (idioms, literally: the inner (person), and: the hidden (person)) the psychological faculty, including intellectual, emotional, and spiritual aspects, in contrast with the purely physical aspects of human existence
s.g: the inner being; the inmost being; inwardly
s.c: In a number of languages it is quite impossible to speak of the psychological faculty of a person as being merely ‘that which is within.’ It is frequently necessary to refer to a particular organ of the body, for example, ‘the heart’ or ‘the liver’ or ‘the spleen.’ In some languages, however, one may refer to this faculty as being ‘the person who stands inside’ or ‘the real person’ or even ‘the other person.’|In ⟦Luke 17:21|Luke 17:21⟧ the phrase ἐντὸς ὑμῶν in the statement ἰδοὺ γὰρ ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ἐντὸς ὑμῶν ἐστιν look, God’s reign is within you may constitute a reference to the same inner being designated by the phrases ὁ ἔσω and ὁ ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ. On this basis some scholars have suggested that the phrase ἐντὸς ὑμῶν can be interpreted as a potentiality for participation and hence be translated within your grasp, but it is more likely that one should understand the phrase ἐντὸς ὑμῶν in ⟦Luke 17:21|Luke 17:21⟧ as a spacial relationship, for example, ‘in your midst’ or ‘among you’ (see LN 83.9).

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Particular Patterns of Behavior
s.d: (an idiom, literally: old person, or: former person) the old or former pattern of behavior, in contrast with a new pattern of behavior which people should conform to
s.g: old self; old pattern of life
s.c: In a number of languages one can best render this expression in ⟦Ephesians 4:22|Ephesians 4:22⟧ as ‘don’t live the way you used to.’

s.d: (a Semitic idiom, literally: sons of men) human beings (equivalent in denotative meaning to {L:ἄνθρωπος<SDBG:ἄνθρωπος:000000>}[a], {D:9.1})
s.c: It is rare indeed that one can reproduce literally the Semitic phrase ‘sons of men,’ since the expression is likely to be interpreted as relating only to the male offspring of fathers.

s.d: a title with Messianic implications used by Jesus concerning himself
s.c: This title ‘Son of Man’ served not only to affirm but also to hide Christ’s Messianic role.|In a number of languages there are serious complications involved in a literal translation of υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ‘Son of Man.’ In the first place, this is likely to be understood in a more or less literal sense of ‘son of a man’ and thus a denial of the virgin birth. Such is particularly true in languages which have two words for ‘son,’ one meaning ‘son of a man’ and the other, ‘son of a woman.’ Under such circumstances, a literal translation would be a clear denial of the virgin birth.

s.d: (the Greek equivalent of the Latin proconsul) an official ruling over a province traditionally under the control of the Roman senate
to cause something to become loose
to desert or forsake a person and thus leave that individual uncared for
to stop doing something, with the implication of complete cessation
s.g: to give up; to stop; to quit

s.dp: Activities Involving Liquids or Masses › Use of Liquids
s.d: pertaining to not being washed

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a prophetess

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a Jewish high priest

s.dp: Understand › Lack of Capacity for Understanding
s.d: pertaining to unwillingness to use one’s mental faculties in order to understand
s.c: As in the case of ἀσύνετος (LN 32.49), the meaning of ἀνόητος is that people presumably would not use their capacity for understanding and as a result, thought and behaved foolishly. ἀνόητος does not imply the mental state of being an idiot or imbecile.

s.dp: Understand › Lack of Capacity for Understanding
s.d: the state of being devoid of understanding
s.g: to lack understanding; absence of understanding
s.c: ἄνοια does not imply in ⟦2 Timothy 3:9|2 Timothy 3:9⟧ that people are incapable of understanding, but that they evidently are unwilling to understand.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Anger, Be Indignant With
s.d: a state of such extreme anger as to suggest an incapacity to use one’s mind
to cause something to be open (see also discussion at {D:79.111}){N:001}
(an idiom, literally: ears open, or possibly: hearing opens) to become able to hear{N:002}
s.g: to regain one’s hearing; to have one’s hearing restored
s.c: In some languages it may be relatively meaningless to translate literally ‘his ears were opened,’ since this might mean nothing more than the removal of some wax from the ear channel. It may therefore be necessary to translate ‘his ears were made so that he could hear again’ or ‘his lack of hearing was healed.’

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to open a door) to make possible some opportunity
(Semitic idiom, literally: to open the mouth) to begin to speak in a somewhat formal and systematic manner
s.g: to address; to start speaking; to begin to speak; to utter

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to open the eyes) to cause someone to be able to see
s.g: to open the eyes; to cause a blind person to see
s.c: A strictly literal translation of ἀνοίγω τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς ‘to open the eyes’ may be entirely misleading since it would imply simply opening the eyelids. It is accordingly much better to translate as ‘to cause to see.’

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to open the mouth to) to speak the complete truth to someone
s.g: to be completely open with; to conceal nothing from; to speak the whole truth to

s.d: to rebuild something which has been destroyed
(Semitic idiom, literally: opening of the mouth) to begin to speak in a somewhat formal and systematic manner
s.g: to address; to start speaking; to begin to speak; to utter

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Act Lawlessly
s.d: to behave with complete disregard for the laws or regulations of a society
s.g: to live lawlessly; lawlessness; lawless living
s.c: In some languages one may translate ἀνομία in ⟦Matthew 13:41|Matthew 13:41⟧ as ‘to live as though there were no laws,’ ‘to refuse completely to obey the laws,’ or ‘to live as one who despises all laws.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Act Lawlessly
s.d: (derivative of {L:ἀνομία<SDBG:ἀνομία:000000>} ‘to live lawlessly,’ {D:88.139}) pertaining to living without regard to law, in the sense of refusing to obey laws
pertaining to being without the Law (specifically the first five books of the OT)
s.c: Even from the two contexts of ⟦1 Corinthians 9:21|1 Corinthians 9:21⟧ and ⟦Romans 2:12|Romans 2:12⟧, it should be clear that ἄνομος and ἀνόμως carry quite different implications in different contexts. In ⟦1 Corinthians 9:21|1 Corinthians 9:21⟧ a phrase such as ‘without the Law’ must be understood in the sense of ‘not being under obligation to the Law’ or ‘not being bound by the Law,’ and so ⟦1 Corinthians 9:21|1 Corinthians 9:21⟧ must be translated in a number of languages as ‘with those who are not bound by the Law, I live as one who is not bound by the Law,’ referring in these instances to the Law of Moses. It is important, however, in rendering the expression ‘not bound by the Law’ to avoid a phrase which would mean ‘lawless’ or ‘heedless of the Law.’ In the case of ⟦Romans 2:12|Romans 2:12⟧, the phrase ‘without the Law’ must refer to those who are ignorant of the Law and thus are not bound by it, and so ⟦Romans 2:12|Romans 2:12⟧ must be rendered in some languages as ‘those who sin without knowing anything about the Law are lost, but quite apart from any relationship to the Law.’|For another interpretation of ἄνομος in ⟦1 Corinthians 9:21|1 Corinthians 9:21⟧, see LN 11.42.

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Religious
s.d: a non-Jew who lives completely without reference to the Jewish Law
s.c: For another interpretation of ἄνομος in ⟦1 Corinthians 9:21|1 Corinthians 9:21⟧, see LN 33.57.|In a number of contexts, it may be best to speak of ‘Gentiles’ as ‘those who are not Jews.’ In some languages the equivalent of ‘Gentiles’ is simply ‘foreigners,’ but one must be very certain that the use of a term meaning ‘foreigners’ will actually designate non-Jews rather than those people who do not speak the particular receptor language.|It would be a serious mistake to render ἄνομος as ‘lawless’ on the basis of its etymology. To speak of a ‘lawless person’ is to imply that he transgresses existing laws rather than being one who is not subject to the Mosaic Law.

s.d: pertaining to being without the Law (specifically the first five books of the OT)
s.c: Even from the two contexts of ⟦1 Corinthians 9:21|1 Corinthians 9:21⟧ and ⟦Romans 2:12|Romans 2:12⟧, it should be clear that ἄνομος and ἀνόμως carry quite different implications in different contexts. In ⟦1 Corinthians 9:21|1 Corinthians 9:21⟧ a phrase such as ‘without the Law’ must be understood in the sense of ‘not being under obligation to the Law’ or ‘not being bound by the Law,’ and so ⟦1 Corinthians 9:21|1 Corinthians 9:21⟧ must be translated in a number of languages as ‘with those who are not bound by the Law, I live as one who is not bound by the Law,’ referring in these instances to the Law of Moses. It is important, however, in rendering the expression ‘not bound by the Law’ to avoid a phrase which would mean ‘lawless’ or ‘heedless of the Law.’ In the case of ⟦Romans 2:12|Romans 2:12⟧, the phrase ‘without the Law’ must refer to those who are ignorant of the Law and thus are not bound by it, and so ⟦Romans 2:12|Romans 2:12⟧ must be rendered in some languages as ‘those who sin without knowing anything about the Law are lost, but quite apart from any relationship to the Law.’
